results.quote: Aurignacian, about 43,000–33,000 years ago, is the first Upper Palaeolithic technocomplex
results.claim: The Aurignacian dates to approximately 43,000–33,000 years ago and is the first Upper Palaeolithic technocomplex to spread across most of Europe
results.reason: Multiple sources confirm the Aurignacian is dated to ~43,000-33,000 years ago and is the first Upper Palaeolithic technocomplex associated with modern humans in Europe (Nature Communications 2024; Springer Encyclopedia 2020; French Ministry of Culture).

results.quote: Hohle Fels female figurine, carved from mammoth ivory, is at least 35,000 years old
results.claim: The Hohle Fels female figurine is at least 35,000 years old
results.reason: Conard (2009) in Nature 459, 248-252 reports the figurine was produced at least 35,000 calendar years ago. Verified via PubMed (PMID: 19444215) and Nature website.

results.quote: Most Aurignacian marks, however, are not figurative. They are notches, lines, dots and crosses
results.claim: Most Aurignacian marks are non-figurative notches, lines, dots, and crosses on tools, ornaments, and stone blocks
results.reason: SignBase paper (Dutkiewicz et al. 2020, Scientific Data) identifies ~30 sign types including line, notch, dot, cross as the most frequent. Notch (254), line (174), cross (38), dot (15) are the top types per presentation materials.

results.quote: Repeated sequences of such marks have been read as possible notational or information-storage devices
results.claim: Repeated sequences of Aurignacian marks have been interpreted as possible notational or information-storage devices
results.reason: The paper cites McPherron et al. (2022) for this claim, but McPherron et al. (2022) is about 'Machine learning, bootstrapping, null models, and why we are still not 100% sure which bone surface modifications were made by crocodiles' (J. Hum. Evol. 164:103071) - a paper on crocodile bite marks, not notational systems. The notational interpretation originates with Marshack (1964, 1972) and is discussed in Bentz & Dutkiewicz (2026, PNAS) and Bacon et al. (2023, Cambridge Archaeol. J.).
results.suggest: Replace citation with Marshack (1964/1972) or Bentz & Dutkiewicz (2026) or Bacon et al. (2023) for notational system claims.

results.quote: If they were shared conventions, their repertoires might differ between regions, as personal ornaments do
results.claim: If Aurignacian marks were shared conventions, their sign repertoires might differ between regions, similar to personal ornaments
results.reason: Vanhaeren & d'Errico (2006, J. Archaeol. Sci. 33:1105-1128) analyzed 157 bead types at 98 Aurignacian sites and found geographically cohesive sets with distinct ornament repertoires, interpreted as reflecting ethno-linguistic diversity. This supports the analogy.

results.quote: SignBase v1.0 (Bentz et al., 2020) records 531 Aurignacian mobile objects from 65 sites in 13 countries
results.claim: SignBase v1.0 contains 531 Aurignacian mobile objects from 65 sites across 13 countries
results.reason: SignBase paper (Dutkiewicz et al. 2020) confirms 531 objects from 65 sites. However, the paper lists sites in ~9-10 countries (France, Germany, Belgium, Czech Republic, Spain, Italy/Sicily, Israel, Iraq, Russia/Ukraine by Black Sea), not 13. The '13 countries' figure may include additional countries not explicitly listed in the paper abstract.
results.suggest: Verify the exact country count from the full dataset or clarify which 13 countries are included.

results.quote: SignBase v1.0 (Bentz et al., 2020) records 531 Aurignacian mobile objects
results.claim: The Methods section claim of 531 total objects in SignBase is consistent with the data source description
results.reason: The Methods section claim of 531 objects matches the SignBase paper (Dutkiewicz et al. 2020) which states '531 mobile objects carrying geometric signs from 65 Aurignacian sites'.
